title: USA Today sues OpenAI for copyright infringement over AI training
key_facts: USA Today Co. and several local newspapers it owns are suing OpenAI.
The suit claims OpenAI copied 'hundreds of thousands' of articles to train its AI models.
Filed Thursday 8 Oct 2026; damages sought are more than $250 million.
The complaint says OpenAI never asked permission and built products worth hundreds of billions of dollars on the content.

Other plaintiffs against OpenAI include The New York Times, The Intercept, Ziff Davis, CBC/Radio-Canada, Encyclopaedia Britannica, Merriam-Webster, The Seattle Times and a coalition of nearly 400 local newspapers.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to The Verge's request for comment.
quote_evidence: USA Today Co., along with the several local newspapers it owns, is suing OpenAI over claims that the company copied “hundreds of thousands” of articles to train its AI models, as reported earlier by Reuters.
“OpenAI’s commercial success rests on large-scale copyright infringement,” USA Today Co.’s lawsuit claims.
why_it_matters_hint: Another large publisher is asking a court to decide whether training AI on news articles without permission is lawful.
notes: Reuters article blocked here (HTTP 401); text read at The Verge, which credits Reuters ('as reported earlier by Reuters'). Forbes and Bloomberg Law carry the same story. OpenAI had not commented when The Verge asked.
